lines.text: the derivative is not a number at a point — it is a function in its own right
the slope at a point is the rate of change there
lines.note: the slope is quoted, not measured: it reads cos(x) because the curve was chosen as sin — so this room shows a rate only for functions already differentiated on paper, and never takes the limit it is named for.

note_src.quote: var slope: float = cos(x_curve) * amplitude  # dy/dx = cos(x) * amplitude (in curve units)

lines.text: velocity is the derivative of position — motion is the visible rate at which where-you-are becomes …
lines.note: the arrow points along a chord to a point 0.05 radians ahead: the puck must be read where it has not arrived, and the chord cuts the corner hardest at the bend the artifact exists to show.

note_src.quote: # Finite-difference velocity: tangent via a small angular step. ... var v := (p_ahead - p) / 0.05  # approximate dP/da

lines.text: a derivative in more than one dimension is not one number but a choice of direction
lines.note: the two arrows measure the hill only along axes someone laid over it — rotate the grid and both numbers change while the ground does not: a partial derivative is a property of the question, not the surface.

note_src.quote: a derivative in more than one dimension is not one number but a choice of direction — you differentiate with respect to whichever axis you think to ask about

lines.text: the integral is accumulation — where the derivative asks how fast
lines.note: the smooth fill is eighty strips: the room promises a boundary swept continuously and ships a comb fine enough to pass for one, so its continuity is an integer anyone can raise or lower.

note_src.quote: the continuous limit is reachable by raising `samples` instead

lines.text: area under a curve has no single recipe — left
lines.note: the exact area is a limit no pump can reach — this hall runs four strips to thirty-two and asserts where infinitely many would land, so every integral downstream is a promise nobody here audits.

note_src.quote: Here the chapter admits its method: the exact is approached, not possessed.

lines.text: a field is not one arrow but a rule that hands you an arrow wherever you stand
lines.note: a field owes a vector to every point and can afford ninety-six arrows: between them the rule is taken on trust, from a stream function chosen by someone the room never names.

note_src.quote: Every cell's arrow was authored, and the author is nowhere visible.

lines.text: a field is invisible until a body moves through it — the particle is how the field speaks
lines.note: the trails are not memory: each is the field integrated backwards from where the particle stands now, so under the scrolling field the room hands every body a past it never had.

note_src.quote: It is therefore a streamline of the instantaneous field, not a pathline — the two differ under `cells`, which scrolls

lines.text: differentiation and integration are the same bridge walked in opposite directions
lines.note: the beam reads f(b) − f(a) over a deck that is a symmetric parabola, so the ends sit level and the theorem the chapter closes on says 0 = 0 in twenty-six rooms.

note_src.quote: This bridge has been labelled with a theorem that, on its own geometry, reads 0 = 0.
